passed.title: Filter drops rows whose predicate evaluates to null
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.filter` keeps only rows where the predicate evaluates to True. Rows where it evaluates to `null` are discarded too. In Polars any comparison involving a null gives `null`, not boolean True or False, so `pl.col("a") != 1` silently drops the null rows as well. Use `Expr.ne_missing`, or add an explicit `| pl.col("a").is_null()`, when nulls must survive the filter.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, None], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]})

# Wrong: the null row is dropped because null != 1 evaluates to null
wrong = lf.filter(pl.col("a") != 1).collect()
print(wrong["b"].to_list())

# Right: null-aware comparison keeps the null row
right = lf.filter(pl.col("a").ne_missing(1)).collect()
print(right["b"].to_list())

# Equivalent explicit form
also_right = lf.filter((pl.col("a") != 1) | pl.col("a").is_null()).collect()
print(also_right["b"].to_list())

passed.title: NaN and null are different: drop_nulls/fill_null ignore NaN
passed.trap: In pandas, NaN is the missing-value marker. In Polars, a floating-point NaN is a real value and is distinct from `null`. `LazyFrame.drop_nulls` and `LazyFrame.fill_null` leave NaN untouched. `LazyFrame.drop_nans` and `LazyFrame.fill_nan` only act on NaN. To treat both as missing, chain the two calls, or convert NaN to null first with `fill_nan(None)`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [1.0, float("nan"), None]})

# drop_nulls keeps the NaN row
print(lf.drop_nulls().collect()["x"].to_list())
# Chain both to drop every kind of missing value
print(lf.drop_nulls().drop_nans().collect()["x"].to_list())

# fill_null does not touch NaN
print(lf.fill_null(0.0).collect()["x"].to_list())
# Convert NaN to null first, then fill everything
print(lf.fill_nan(None).fill_null(0.0).collect()["x"].to_list())

passed.title: LazyFrame.count counts non-null values per column, not rows
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.count` returns a one-row frame holding the number of non-null elements in each column. It is not the number of rows: a column containing nulls reports fewer than the frame height. To get the row count, use `lf.select(pl.len())`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, None, 6]})

# Per-column non-null counts, NOT the row count
print(lf.count().collect().row(0))

# Actual number of rows
print(lf.select(pl.len()).collect().item())

passed.title: LazyFrame.describe collects eagerly and returns a DataFrame
passed.trap: Unlike most LazyFrame methods, `LazyFrame.describe` does not stay lazy. It runs the whole query and returns a `DataFrame`, which can be expensive on a large scan. Do not chain further lazy operations after it. Its output is also documented as not stable across versions, so do not parse it programmatically. For statistics you rely on in code, build explicit aggregations with `LazyFrame.select`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4.0, None, 6.0]})

summary = lf.describe()  # executes the query immediately
print(isinstance(summary, pl.DataFrame))

# Stable, lazy, programmatic statistics instead
stats = lf.select(
    pl.col("a").mean().alias("a_mean"),
    pl.col("b").null_count().alias("b_nulls"),
).collect()
print(stats.row(0))

passed.title: group_by does not preserve group order unless maintain_order=True
passed.trap: With the default `maintain_order=False`, `LazyFrame.group_by` does not guarantee that groups come out in any particular order, so tests and `head()` calls that assume an order can break. Pass `maintain_order=True` to keep the order consistent with the input (first appearance), or call `sort` on the result explicitly. Per the docstring, `maintain_order=True` is slower and blocks the possibility of running on the streaming engine.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"k": ["b", "a", "b", "c"], "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

# Order of first appearance in the input
ordered = lf.group_by("k", maintain_order=True).agg(pl.col("v").sum()).collect()
print(ordered["k"].to_list())

# Or sort explicitly after an unordered group_by
sorted_out = lf.group_by("k").agg(pl.col("v").sum()).sort("k").collect()
print(sorted_out["k"].to_list(), sorted_out["v"].to_list())

passed.title: join never matches null keys by default and does not guarantee row order
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.join` uses `nulls_equal=False` by default, so null keys never match each other. Rows keyed on null disappear from an inner join; pandas `merge` does match NaN keys. Set `nulls_equal=True` if nulls should match; this parameter was called `join_nulls` before 1.24. The default `maintain_order=None` does not promise any output order, so `sort` the result if order matters.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

left = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1, None], "l": ["x", "y"]})
right = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1, None], "r": ["p", "q"]})

# Default: the null keys do not match
default = left.join(right, on="k").sort("l").collect()
print(default.height, default["r"].to_list())

# Opt in to matching nulls
matched = left.join(right, on="k", nulls_equal=True).sort("l").collect()
print(matched.height, matched["r"].to_list())

passed.title: bottom_k output is unordered and the direction flag is reverse, not descending
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.bottom_k` and `LazyFrame.top_k` return the selected rows in no guaranteed order. Call `LazyFrame.sort` afterwards if you need them ranked. To flip the direction, pass `reverse=True`. These methods have no `descending` keyword. Non-null values are always preferred over nulls, whatever the value of `reverse`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"name": ["a", "b", "c", "d"], "score": [5, None, 3, 2]})

# Sort explicitly to get a ranked result
low = lf.bottom_k(2, by="score").sort("score").collect()
print(low["name"].to_list())

# reverse=True picks the largest; the null score is never chosen
high = lf.bottom_k(2, by="score", reverse=True).sort("score", descending=True).collect()
print(high["name"].to_list())

passed.title: fetch and approx_n_unique on LazyFrame are deprecated
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.fetch` is deprecated. Use `LazyFrame.head` followed by `LazyFrame.collect` instead, but note the two are not equivalent. `fetch` limited the rows read by every scan, so filters and joins could return fewer rows or none. `head` limits the final result. `LazyFrame.approx_n_unique` is also deprecated; use `lf.select(pl.all().approx_n_unique())` with `Expr.approx_n_unique`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 2, 3], "b": [1, 1, 1, 1]})

# Replacement for lf.fetch(2): limit the final output, then collect
print(lf.head(2).collect().rows())

# Replacement for lf.approx_n_unique()
print(lf.select(pl.all().approx_n_unique()).collect().row(0))
